title: Node Modules and npm: CommonJS vs ESM, package.json, Semver, Lockfiles and Scripts
summary: Quick revision notes on how Node loads code (CommonJS vs ES modules, require vs import) and how npm manages it (package.json, dependency types, semver, lockfiles, scripts). Ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: CommonJS vs ES Modules
points: CommonJS loads with require() and exports with module.exports; it runs synchronously, so the whole file executes at the call and the result is cached in require.cache. ESM uses static import/export, is parsed before it runs, and loads asynchronously.

Comparison: require() can sit inside an if or a function and take a computed path. import is hoisted to the top level and needs a literal string. Use dynamic import('./x.js') for conditional loading, which returns a Promise.
Node picks the system per file. .mjs is always ESM and .cjs is always CJS. For .js, "type": "module" in the nearest package.json makes it ESM, and the default ("commonjs") makes it CJS.

Example: const fs = require('fs'); module.exports = { run } versus import fs from 'fs'; export const run = () => {}. ESM relative imports need the file extension (./util.js). ESM has no __dirname or require; use import.meta.url or import.meta.dirname instead.

Interview Point: (1) Why can't you require() an ES module in older Node, and what does import() solve? (2) How does Node decide whether a .js file is CJS or ESM? (3) CJS exports are copies of values while ESM exports are live bindings. What does that change?

chapters.title: package.json Essentials
points: name and version identify the package; both are required to publish, and name must be lowercase with no spaces. private: true blocks accidental npm publish.

main is the CJS entry file, and "type": "module" switches .js files to ESM. The exports field maps subpaths and conditions ("import" vs "require") and blocks deep imports of anything it does not list. It overrides main in modern Node.
npm init -y creates a default package.json, and npm init asks questions. Example: { "name": "app", "version": "1.0.0", "type": "module", "scripts": { "start": "node index.js" } }.

Mistake: a trailing comma or a comment breaks package.json, because it is strict JSON. `Cannot use import statement outside a module` appears when a .js file with import syntax is treated as CommonJS (older Node, or "type": "commonjs"); Node 22.7+ detects ESM syntax when "type" is missing but warns, so add "type": "module". Editing by hand without running install leaves the lockfile out of sync.
Interview Point: (1) What do main, module and exports each do, and which wins? (2) What does "type": "module" change? (3) Why mark an app private: true?

chapters.title: dependencies vs devDependencies
points: dependencies are needed at runtime in production (express, react). devDependencies are only for building, testing and linting (jest, eslint, typescript, vite). Install flags: npm i pkg writes to dependencies, and npm i -D pkg writes to devDependencies.
npm install --omit=dev (older: --production) or NODE_ENV=production skips devDependencies. When someone installs your library, only its dependencies are installed, never its devDependencies.

Comparison: peerDependencies mean the host app must supply the package (a React plugin needs react). Since npm 7 they are installed automatically. optionalDependencies may fail to install without breaking the install. Use dependencies for what you import and peerDependencies for what you share with the host.

Mistake: putting a build tool the production server needs (for example typescript when you compile on deploy) in devDependencies, then the production install omits it and the build fails. The reverse mistake, test libraries in dependencies, bloats images and installs.
Interview Point: (1) What is the difference between dependencies and devDependencies at deploy time? (2) When should something be a peerDependency? (3) What does npm install --omit=dev do?

chapters.title: Semver and Lockfiles
points: Semver is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. PATCH is a bug fix, MINOR adds a backward-compatible feature, and MAJOR is a breaking change.
Range prefixes: ^1.2.3 allows 1.x.x at or above 1.2.3 (the npm default). ~1.2.3 allows 1.2.x only. 1.2.3 is exact. Caveat: ^0.2.3 allows only 0.2.x, because below 1.0.0 a minor bump may break.

package-lock.json records the exact resolved version, tarball URL and integrity hash of the whole tree, including transitive dependencies. Commit it. npm install respects it and may update it. npm ci installs strictly from it, deletes node_modules first, and fails if package.json and the lock disagree, which makes it the right command for CI.

Mistake: deleting the lockfile, or committing two (npm and yarn) lockfiles, gives each machine different versions, which causes 'works on my machine'. Never hand-edit the lockfile. Use npm update to move within ranges and npm outdated to see what can change.
Interview Point: (1) What does ^ allow versus ~? (2) Why commit package-lock.json, and how does npm ci differ from npm install? (3) What does semver promise and where does it break down?

chapters.title: npm Scripts and Everyday Commands
points: The scripts field maps names to shell commands. npm run <name> runs one, and test, start and stop can skip run (npm test, npm start). Local binaries in node_modules/.bin are on the PATH during a script, so "lint": "eslint ." works without a global install.

Lifecycle hooks: pre<name> and post<name> run automatically around a script (pretest, postbuild). prepare runs after a local npm install and before publish, and is the usual place to build or install git hooks.

Passing arguments: npm run test -- --watch sends everything after -- to the script. Chain with && so each step must succeed ("build": "tsc && node dist"). npx <tool> runs a package binary without installing it permanently.

Everyday commands: npm install (all), npm i pkg, npm i -D pkg, npm uninstall pkg, npm ls, npm outdated, npm update. Mistakes: installing tools globally with -g and hitting version drift, using Unix-only commands like rm -rf in scripts that Windows teammates run, and forgetting `--` before forwarded flags.
Interview Point: (1) Why does a script find eslint without a global install? (2) What are pre and post hooks, and what is prepare for? (3) How do you pass flags through npm run?

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Modules and npm
points: Modules: CJS is require/module.exports, sync, dynamic, and the default for .js. ESM is import/export, static and async, needs "type": "module" or .mjs, and needs file extensions on relative imports. CJS loads ESM through import(), or with require() on Node 22.12+ and 20.19+ (no top-level await), and ESM can import CJS by default import.
Dependency types: dependencies = runtime. devDependencies = build and test (-D). peerDependencies = the host app supplies it. Install without dev: npm i --omit=dev.
Semver: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, ^ = same major (default), ~ = same minor, no prefix = exact, and ^0.x pins the minor. The lockfile is committed and never hand-edited. npm ci in CI, npm install locally.
Scripts: npm run <name>, with test/start shorthand, pre/post hooks, and args via `--`. Local .bin is on the PATH, and npx runs one-off tools.

Fix-it list: `Cannot use import statement outside a module` means add "type": "module" or use .mjs. `require is not defined` and `__dirname is not defined` mean you are in ESM, so use import() and import.meta. `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` usually means a missing file extension. A lock mismatch error from npm ci means run npm install and commit the updated lockfile.
